newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angolan peace at peril in Zaire domino effect.
newsitem.headline: Angolan peace at peril in Zaire domino effect.

text.p: Angola lurched towards crisis on Friday with a government warning that new fighting involving the former rebel movement UNITA could wreck the fragile peace process and restart a civil war that went on for 20 years.

The flareup is directly linked to last month's defeat of the regime of Mobutu Sese Seko in neighbouring Zaire, a longtime ally of UNITA. Mobutu was toppled by Laurent Kabila, who has the staunch support of the Angolan government.

Military sources say the government and UNITA have thrown many troops into recent battles. The army was using tanks and artillery and the ex-rebels were firing mortar barrages, in what was described as the worst fighting since a 1994 peace pact.
With its key ally Mobutu now in exile, UNITA said in a statement from its office in Rome that it was ready for immediate top-level talks to end the fighting.

UNITA said its leader Jonas Savimbi was prepared to meet President Jose Eduardo dos Santos of Angola in Italy, where dos Santos is currently on holiday. The offer was in response to an appeal from U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan for talks "with the precise aim of overcoming the current deep crisis".
In its first official statement since the fighting began three weeks ago, the Angolan government said UNITA was gathering soldiers and war material, threatening the peace accord.
UNITA's actions "could put in danger the Lusaka protocols, with all the grave consequences that would entail", it said.

"The United Nations must adopt measures to stop these belligerent intentions...the government has no intentions of returning to war...the government cannot ignore its own responsibilities to secure the frontier," it added.

The Angolan government denies it is taking advantage of UNITA's loss of a major ally who guarded the rebel movement's back door beyond the northern Angolan border with Zaire, and gave it logistics routes and a market for diamonds.

But analysts say it has seized the opportunity to roll back UNITA's grip on the northern diamond-rich areas which yield hundreds of millions of dollars annually, if not to deliver a military knockout blow to its old enemy.

The government's warning on Friday coincided with reports, which could not be independently confirmed, that UNITA was flying in arms from Bulgaria and reoccupying bases it gave up under the peace pact.
An analyst who declined to be named said UNITA was flying in arms from Bulgaria to its Andulo stronghold in DC-10 aircraft, after extending the strip there to accomodate the planes.
An Angolan police commander told national radio that UNITA was reactivating old bases in northeastern Lunda Sul province, which had been decommissioned under the peace accord.
He reported the movement of large numbers of men and materials, including supplies flown from Savimbi's Bailundo stronghold and said Zaireans loyal to Mobutu were helping.
The United Nations special envoy to Angola, Alouin Blondin Beye, said he had ordered an investigation into the clashes and expected a report next week.

He pointed out that no one could stop the Angolans going back to war if they wanted to and said that, if the situation deteriorated, he would suggest to the Security Council that the U.N.'s 6,000 peacekeepers delay a withdrawal planned for autumn.

The envoy stressed he was not yet ready to take a position and noted that some members of UNITA -- which appears increasingly divided -- have taken up their role in a national unity parliament which convened earlier this week.

U.N. force commander Phillip Sibanda on Friday went to the northeastern town of Nzage where fighting has intensified, and estimated that 14 army soldiers were killed and 90 wounded in nearby clashes. There were no figures on UNITA casualties.

A mission including military attaches from the United States, Portugal and Russia -- the countries helping to oversee Angola's peace process -- travelled to other areas in the north to verify reports of UNITA troop movements.

Thousands of UNITA troops were reportedly returning to Angola from the former Zaire, where they made a vain bid to prop up the Mobutu regime. Hutu militiamen who fled Rwanda and took refuge in Mobutu's Zaire were said to be among them.
